done.why: The Troll Room's east passage is unfinished and the west hole goes nowhere yet, so I had nowhere further to go.

about: A Zork-like adventure. You start outside a white house, get in through a window, collect a lantern and sword, open a trap door to a cellar and kill a troll. Past that the map runs out.

ending.what: No ending. The explorable area stopped at the Troll Room.

moments.note: Longer sentences like 'go to the front door and try to open it' got 'That sentence isn't one I recognize', with no hint of what it would accept.
'go in through the window' was rejected. I had to guess that 'west' would take me through.
The trap door crashed shut behind me and I heard it being barred.
I killed the troll with one blow. That felt too easy, but it was satisfying.
The note 'Back soon. -- The Management.' left by the unfinished passage was funny.
Attacking again gave 'You can't see any such thing.' This was expected, since the troll was gone, but it was not explained.

wished: To say plain sentences, such as 'go in through the window', and have them understood.
To have more places to explore past the Troll Room.
Some hint about what to aim for.

lines.line: Your sword is glowing with a faint blue glow.
lines.why: This was a subtle warning that danger was close, and it paid off in the next room.

lines.line: Someone has left a pick leaning against the rock, and a note: "Back soon. -- The Management."
lines.why: A funny way to say an area isn't finished.

lines.line: With a great effort, the rug is moved to one side of the room, revealing the dusty cover of a closed trap door.

fun.why: Opening up the house and finding the cellar was fun, but the game ended quickly at the unfinished area.

engagement.why: I was hooked while exploring the house, then hit a dead end.

difficulty.why: Everything I tried worked, and the troll died in one hit. The only friction was the parser rejecting some phrasings.

interestingness.why: The setting is familiar and the details are charming, but the explorable area is small.

prose.why: The prose is concise and atmospheric.
